Whether the market moved toward the side we took between the pick being issued and kickoff. It is not a record and it is not profit: a pick can beat the close and still lose. How our number compares with the market's

Across 164 games whose number was frozen before kickoff, ours missed the final margin by 11.8 points on average and the market's by 11.0. We were closer in 72, the market in 91. The backtest, which is walk-forward over four seasons, has the market ahead; a small in-season sample that disagrees with that is not evidence against it.

282 earlier rows are left out of these figures. Our number on those was worked out after the final score, from ratings that had already been refitted on that same game, so it was a fit rather than a forecast and cannot honestly be compared with the market. They are still in ledger.csv, marked post.

Two grades, not one

Every market gets two readings, because they answer different questions and this model is far better at one of them.

Confidence How likely the call is to happen. Nothing to do with the price. The simulation's answer, corrected by what calls like it actually did over 2017-2025, walk-forward, FBS vs FBS, real closing lines. Bands: A at 75% or better, B at 65%, C at 55%, D below.
Value How far that corrected probability sits above the break-even the price demands. A spread or total carries no price in this feed, so it uses the standard 52.4% figure. A moneyline has a real price and uses it. Bands: A at +2 points or better, B at +1, C at break-even, D below.
Grade The two weighted together, confidence 60% and value 40%. Those weights are the only chosen numbers in the scheme. They sit in model_state.json next to the measured ones so it is obvious which is which.
Confidence floor Nothing under 40% likely can grade above D, whatever the price offers. This floor is chosen, not measured: no bucket at the BOTTOM lost with its whole interval below zero, so there is no measured floor and the chosen one stands. The buckets that did lose outright were 50-100%, which a floor cannot reach. The backtest buckets moneyline bets by corrected probability and asks whether each bucket made money; where the bottom buckets lost with their whole 95% interval below zero, the top of that run is the floor. An 8% shot at +1800 clears its break-even on paper and used to reach a C on value alone. At that probability the model would have to be right to a fraction of a point for the value figure to mean anything, and nothing measures it that finely.

Why two and not the old single score. The old grade was one score out of 100, seventy points for the win probability and thirty for value over the price. On a spread or a total that was one number counted twice: the feed carries the number and no price, so the market's implied probability is fifty percent by construction and the value term was the win probability restated. The moneyline was the only market where the two were genuinely different. Splitting them makes that visible instead of hiding it inside an average.

Why a simulated probability is not a probability

The simulation says what would happen if our number were right. Whether it is right is a separate question, and the backtest answers it by fitting, for each market, the line that maps what the model claimed onto what actually happened.

marketwhat the fit says
outrightfitted slope +1.13 over 6,019 games, clear of zero, so this probability carries real information
model gap earlyfitted slope -0.12 over 1,558 games, not distinguishable from zero, so this reads as close to a coin flip whatever the model says
model gap latefitted slope -0.20 over 4,461 games, not distinguishable from zero, so this reads as close to a coin flip whatever the model says
total modelfitted slope -0.03 over 6,065 games, not distinguishable from zero, so this reads as close to a coin flip whatever the model says
price gapfitted slope +0.20 over 355 games, not distinguishable from zero, so this reads as close to a coin flip whatever the model says

Read that table before reading any grade. Predicting the winner works. Beating the number does not. The outright fit clears zero comfortably, so moneyline confidence means something. The spread and total slopes cannot be told apart from zero, which is why their confidence sits near a coin flip however far our number is from the market's. That is the measurement, not a decision.

One thing worth knowing from the same fit: when the model calls a game close to even, the home team actually wins about 45% of the time. The model over-rates home teams in tight games, so road teams in near-even matchups are underrated by roughly the same amount.

What caps a grade

A star means the grade was held back, and hovering it says why. Three things can do it.

A strategy that backtested below break-even cannot grade above C, whatever the simulation says. A market with no backtested record cannot grade above B: confidence may be measured, but whether betting it makes money has never been tested, and an A would claim it had been. A market that has never been calibrated cannot grade above C, because an unchecked probability is a claim about nothing.

Every cap lifts on its own. Re-running the cfb-backtest workflow writes the new record and the new calibration into model_state.json, and every grade here recalculates with nothing to paste. Every number on this tab is read from that file, so the page cannot drift away from the backtest it is quoting. This one was run on 2026-09-09T05:44:42Z over 2017-2025, walk-forward, FBS vs FBS, real closing lines.

Does the window decide the answer?

The backtest starts in 2017 because that is the start of the transfer portal era and betting line coverage thins out before it. That is a judgement, not a measurement, so it is checked rather than trusted: the same headline is re-run on windows that drop the earliest seasons one at a time.

The label changes (loses, no evidence) and the win rate moves with it. The windows starting 2023, 2024, 2025 sit outside the full window's 48.2% to 50.7%, so this is not just a wider interval on fewer games. The start year is doing some of the work and the pooled figure is not safe to quote on its own. Read it the other way too: the recent seasons look better than the pooled record, and they are also the thinnest samples here. Neither reading is established, which is the honest answer until more seasons land.

For reference, the old single score is still computed on every game. On this week's slate it would have graded 36 of 56 spreads an A, on a strategy that backtested below break-even.

The simulation

Every game runs 20,000 times rather than through a single formula. Each run makes two draws.

Our own uncertaintyWe do not know the true line, only our estimate. Each run pulls a true line from a distribution centred on our number with a 7.0-point spread. The NFL card uses 3.0. Ours is more than double because that is what the data says: the standard deviation of our number minus the market's is 7.0 points.
The game itselfGiven that line, the margin is drawn with a standard deviation of about 15.0 points, against the NFL's 13.2, widening for high totals and tightening for low ones. Totals are drawn separately at 13.3 points, against the NFL's 10.4.

The margin tilt is fitted, not assumed: absolute residual = 0.0541 x total + 7.35 over 762 FBS games from 2025, normalised at a total of 52. Wind is not adjusted for, because there is no historical college weather on hand to measure it.

What this tells you

A book's two prices disagreeIts moneyline implies a different spread than the one it posts, so one is stale. Names the better-priced ticket. Says nothing about which side to take. This is the only angle here that needs no model, and the only one currently rated better than AVOID.
Markets point different waysThe best cover and the best value to win outright are different teams. Legitimate: a team can be likely to win without winning by the number.
Our two models disagreeOur ridge rating against SP+. Past 10 points apart, one is badly wrong with no way to tell which. Low information.
blankNothing to say about this game: no pricing inconsistency, no split between the markets, no model disagreement. The column is left empty rather than filled with filler, so anything written in it is worth reading.

Where the numbers come from

Power ratings are an opponent-adjusted ridge regression on game margins, shrunk toward a recruiting-talent prior. Games, lines, talent, SP+, returning production and venues come from CollegeFootballData; weather from Open-Meteo. Injuries, transfers, coaching changes and expert picks are in no dataset and are researched separately into notes.json.

Scope is FBS and FCS. Cross-division games are shown for reference and never given a pick, because a single offset cannot place the two divisions on one reliable scale.

Ratings: opponent-adjusted ridge on game margins, shrunk toward a talent prior. Home field +5.4. FBS over FCS +21.9. Built from 6,274 games across 266 teams. Picks are append-only and keep the number they were issued at. No bet sizing or staking advice appears here by design.
